newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Kiwi dlr thumbs nose at RBNZ signal, closes weaker.
newsitem.headline: Kiwi dlr thumbs nose at RBNZ signal, closes weaker.

text.p: The New Zealand dollar thumbed its nose at a signal to firm from the Governor of the Reserve Bank on Thursday and closed sharply lower.
RBNZ governor Don Brash issued a statement at 1.00 p.m. (0100 GMT) this session, saying monetary conditions had eased too far. The bulk of the recent move had been in the currency.

The Monetary Conditions Index (MCI), which measures the mixture of the 90-day bank bill yield and the kiwi's Trade- Weighted Index, had fallen to 753 -- 72 basis points below the RBNZ's desired level of 825 and 22 points beyond the limit of the bank's stated comfort zone.
Yet the Kiwi rose only briefly in response to Brash's warning, and quickly resumed its downward spiral as offshore investors sold the currency.
The Kiwi closed at US$0.6755/62 and at 66.27 on the TWI, down from 0.6780/87 and 66.52 at the open.
"It's been a very strange day. It's been the first time that Dr Brash has issued a comment of that nature and our market hasn't reacted to it," said a bank chief dealer.
"If anything it's done the opposite, and that's got to be a concern to be honest."
The Kiwi was trading around the 0.6760 level when Brash made the comments. It traded up to 0.6785 on the statement but was sold straight back down again, dealers said.
They said the New Zealand economy was generally perceived to be very weak, despite the RBNZ's prediction that growth had bottomed in the March quarter and rebounded in the June quarter.

"The market feeling is obviously that conditions are still too tight. The economy is slower than what the Reserve Bank feels, so the market has continued to push the boundaries, wanting to see what the Reserve Bank's response is going to be," said Phillip Lindberg at Bankers Trust.
One possible solution was for the bank to cut its cash target, which would push interest rates higher and make the Kiwi more attractive to buy.
"Obviously Dr Brash's only way of correcting his MCI if the currency falls off is to put interest rates higher, and if the economy is weak why would he want to do that?" said the chief dealer.
Some dealers cited a trading note from JP Morgan, saying that the Kiwi would fall to 66 U.S. cents by September, which might have also contributed to the negative sentiment.
"I think we're going to test lower. Certainly I think we're looking at testing probably 0.6730," said the chief dealer.
Overnight, the Kiwi was seen trading in a 0.6730-80 range.
